location: Task 2, Produces (lines 320-324) and implementation of allocate()/release() (lines 501-618). Header Rule 3 (line 27). Only one concurrent test exists (lines 405-434), and it races two different orders against one batch.
title: Nothing serialises operations on the same order: double confirm, double cancel, and confirm racing cancel all corrupt stock silently
failure_scenario: FOR UPDATE locks batch rows only. Neither method locks the order row or checks its status, and release() is not idempotent. (1) Double release under READ COMMITTED: batch B (received 500) has order A holding 200 and order C holding 250, so 50 remain. The admin double-clicks cancel on A. tx1 and tx2 both run the plain findMany and both see A's allocation row. tx1 increments B by 200, writes +200 ORDER_OUT and deletes the rows. tx2's increment waits on B's row lock, then applies on top: 50+200+200 = 450. That is under 500, so warehouse_batches_qty_sane passes. tx2's deleteMany hits 0 rows. Result: 200 units of fabricated stock, backed by two +200 ORDER_OUT movements, so ledger and cache agree and ledger-assert stays silent. (2) Double confirm of one order: both requests read PLACED and both call allocate. The stock is decremented twice and two sets of allocation rows are written. At delivery, Task 6 credits the client for every allocation, so the client is credited twice. (3) Admin confirm racing client cancel at PLACED: if the cancel's UPDATE lands last, the order ends CANCELLED/NOT_ALLOCATED while its ORDER_OUT movements and allocations persist. The units are gone from the warehouse permanently and nothing points at them. Task 5's 'confirming twice is refused' and Task 7's 'cancelling twice is refused' are sequential tests, so they pass.

location: Task 2 implementation, allocate() (lines 501-574) vs release() (lines 588-617). Release test's `confirmAnOrderFor(200)` (line 438). Task 1 OrderLine model (lines 144-166): no @@unique([orderId, itemId]).
title: allocate() writes stock and ledger but not the OrderLineAllocation rows that release() and delivery rely on
failure_scenario: allocate() decrements batches and writes ORDER_OUT rows keyed only by refId=orderId. It returns results keyed by itemId and persists no OrderLineAllocation. release() restores ONLY what it finds in order_line_allocations, and Task 6's delivery credits the client ONLY from those rows. Recording the reservation is left to Task 5, outside the 'one code path'. If Task 5 skips a result or maps it to the wrong line, the problem stays silent. Nothing ties an itemId back to a line, and OrderLine has no unique (orderId, itemId). Example: movements exist with no matching allocation rows. A CONFIRMED cancel then releases nothing and the warehouse stays short. Or a delivery credits the client less than the warehouse lost. Ledger and cache agree on both sides. Separately, the plan's release test cannot be written as specified. `confirmAnOrderFor` (and seedBatch, allocateInTx, batchIdOf, releaseInTx) are never defined. The helper would have to re-implement Task 5's allocation-row writing inside the test, so the test ends up checking the test's own logic.

location: Task 1 Step 3, `orders_cancel_disposition_required` (lines 290-296) and its commentary (line 299). CancelDisposition enum doc (lines 79-84). Order.cancelDisposition doc (lines 124-126). Contradicts Task 7's matrix (lines 718-723: dispositionRequired false at PLACED/CONFIRMED).
title: Disposition CHECK is too strict for PLACED/CONFIRMED cancels and too weak to stop a WRITTEN_OFF recorded on goods that never left
failure_scenario: The CHECK requires a disposition on EVERY cancelled order, but the plan never says what PLACED or CONFIRMED cancellations record. The comment says 'ever allocated', which does not match the body. The field doc and the enum doc both say 'required from OUT_FOR_DELIVERY'. The client cancel endpoint takes no disposition. If Task 7 follows its matrix and leaves the disposition null, every client cancel and every CONFIRMED cancel fails with a check violation, surfacing as a 500. No enum value is truthful for a CONFIRMED cancel. NOT_ALLOCATED is false because stock was allocated. RETURNED_TO_WAREHOUSE means 'the driver brought it back' in §7.4. Worse, the CHECK does not tie the disposition to the lifecycle. Admin cancels a CONFIRMED order via `{disposition: 'WRITTEN_OFF'}` (optional at every state per line 708). If the service branches on the disposition, 'WRITTEN_OFF → no movement' applies and goods still physically in the warehouse are removed. Cache and ledger agree, so the result is a permanent phantom loss that is invisible to ledger-assert. If the service branches on status instead, stock is released but the order permanently records a false WRITTEN_OFF. NOT_ALLOCATED on an order that has confirmedAt set is equally accepted.
fix:
Add an enum value for 'released before dispatch' (e.g. `RELEASED_BEFORE_DISPATCH`; update spec §6/§7.4). The server sets it at CONFIRMED and sets NOT_ALLOCATED at PLACED. The admin chooses only at OUT_FOR_DELIVERY. Replace the CHECK with one that uses the lifecycle timestamps; dispatchedAt becomes load-bearing and Task 6 must set it:
```sql
ALTER TABLE "orders" ADD CONSTRAINT "orders_cancel_disposition_coherent" CHECK (
  (("status" = 'CANCELLED') = ("cancelDisposition" IS NOT NULL))
  AND ("status" <> 'CANCELLED' OR "cancelledAt" IS NOT NULL)
  AND ("cancelDisposition" <> 'NOT_ALLOCATED' OR "confirmedAt" IS NULL)
  AND ("cancelDisposition" <> 'RELEASED_BEFORE_DISPATCH' OR ("confirmedAt" IS NOT NULL AND "dispatchedAt" IS NULL))
  AND ("cancelDisposition" NOT IN ('RETURNED_TO_WAREHOUSE','WRITTEN_OFF') OR "dispatchedAt" IS NOT NULL)
);
```
This CHECK also rejects both orderings of the confirm-vs-cancel race in the order-serialisation finding. Step 4 tests: WRITTEN_OFF without dispatchedAt is rejected; NOT_ALLOCATED with confirmedAt is rejected; a disposition on a non-cancelled order is rejected.

location: Task 1 OrderLine (lines 151-154). CHECK `order_lines_qty_sane` (lines 276-278). Task 5 (line 678: admin edits `{ orderLineId, qtyBoxes }`).
title: No approved-quantity field: admin quantity edits either destroy the client's request, break the CHECK, or look like a stock shortfall
failure_scenario: Spec §7.4 lets the admin edit quantities at confirmation, but OrderLine only has requested and fulfilled quantities. Each way of applying an edit fails. (a) Overwrite qtyBoxesRequested/qtyUnitsRequested: the client's original request disappears from the order. Dropping a line (edit to 0) violates `qtyUnitsRequested > 0` and the confirm returns a 500. (b) Keep requested, allocate fewer: qtyUnitsFulfilled < requested is documented as 'a partial fulfilment', so Task 10 tells the clinic the warehouse was short when the admin chose to cut. (c) Edit upward (5 → 7 boxes): fulfilled 700 > requested 500 and the CHECK rejects it. Separately, nothing ties qtyUnitsRequested to qtyBoxesRequested × unitsPerBoxSnapshot. An edit that updates boxes but not units allocates one quantity and bills boxes × price for another, which goes unnoticed.
fix:
Add `qtyBoxesApproved Int?` and `qtyUnitsApproved Int?`, set at confirmation (null means as requested); allocate against approved. CHECKs:
```sql
CHECK ("qtyBoxesRequested" > 0 AND "unitsPerBoxSnapshot" > 0
  AND "qtyUnitsRequested" = "qtyBoxesRequested" * "unitsPerBoxSnapshot"
  AND ("qtyUnitsApproved" IS NULL OR ("qtyUnitsApproved" >= 0 AND "qtyUnitsApproved" = "qtyBoxesApproved" * "unitsPerBoxSnapshot"))
  AND "qtyUnitsFulfilled" BETWEEN 0 AND COALESCE("qtyUnitsApproved", "qtyUnitsRequested"))
```
The UI then distinguishes 'admin changed' (approved < requested) from 'warehouse short' (fulfilled < approved). The §7.9 audit records requested → approved.

location: Task 1 OrderLine `lineTotal` (line 160; semantics undocumented). Task 5 (line 680, 'recompute totalAmount from what was actually fulfilled'; lineTotal not mentioned). Task 4 test 'totalAmount equals the sum of line totals' (line 670).
title: After a partial fulfilment, line totals and the order's cash total disagree
failure_scenario: Two lines of 10 boxes × 5.00 give lineTotal 50 each and totalAmount 100. Line A is short 5 boxes. Task 5 recomputes totalAmount to 75, but lineTotal A stays 50. The driver's sheet and the client's order screen list 50 + 50 = 100 against a cash total of 75. Alternatively, the implementer recomputes the total independently of the lines, and per-line rounding makes them differ by cents when fulfilled units are not whole boxes. That can happen once a partial EXPIRY_WRITEOFF or MANUAL_ADJUST leaves a batch at a non-box multiple. The placement-time test cannot detect either case.
fix: Document in the schema that lineTotal is the billed amount: pricePerBoxSnapshot × requested boxes at PLACED, then pricePerBoxSnapshot × fulfilled units / unitsPerBoxSnapshot rounded half-up to 2dp at CONFIRMED. Always compute totalAmount as Σ lineTotal, never on its own. Add an assertion to Task 5's tests (and a CHECK `"lineTotal" >= 0`) that Σ lineTotal == totalAmount after confirmation. Optionally keep `lineTotalRequested` for display.

location: Task 2 allocate() loop `for (const request of requests)` (line 511) and the FOR UPDATE query (lines 519-527). release() `findMany` with no orderBy (lines 588-597).
title: Lock order is only deterministic within one item; multi-item confirmations and release-vs-allocate deadlock, and FEFO can skip a just-released batch
failure_scenario: The comment claims deadlock safety, but only rows of ONE item are totally ordered. Rows across items are locked in whatever order the caller passes lines. Order A has lines [X, Y] and order B has [Y, X]; confirming both at once: A locks X's batches, B locks Y's, then each waits on the other. PostgreSQL returns 40P01, which adapter-pg maps to TransactionWriteConflict (Prisma P2034), and one confirmation fails with a 500. release() updates batches in arbitrary findMany order, so it can deadlock against allocate the same way. There is also a silent variant: allocate's snapshot is taken before it blocks. If a concurrent release restores an earlier-expiring batch E0 from 0 to 200, E0 did not match `qtyUnitsRemaining > 0` in the snapshot. READ COMMITTED re-checks only rows that already matched, so E0 is never considered. A later-expiring batch ships while E0 stays in the warehouse and moves toward expiry.

location: Header 'Consumes from Phases 0–2' table, AuditService row (line 51). Used by Task 5 ('One transaction: … set CONFIRMED and confirmedAt, audit', line 680) and Task 7.
title: AuditService.record cannot join the confirm/cancel transaction, so the append-only audit log records decisions that were rolled back
failure_scenario: src/audit/audit.service.ts record() always writes through the global `this.prisma.auditLog.create`; it accepts no transaction client. Called inside the confirmation's $transaction callback, it commits immediately on its own pooled connection. The confirmation then fails, for example on the deadlock above, a CHECK violation, or Prisma's 5s interactive-transaction timeout while waiting on a FOR UPDATE, and the transaction rolls back. The audit log now permanently says ORDER_CONFIRMED with edited quantities, or ORDER_CANCELLED with WRITTEN_OFF, for an order that is still PLACED or CONFIRMED. The log has no update or delete path, so the false entry cannot be corrected. If audit is instead called after commit (the Phase 2 BatchesService pattern) and fails, the decision goes unrecorded.
fix: Extend the consumed contract: `record(entry: AuditEntry, db: Prisma.TransactionClient | PrismaService = this.prisma)`, and pass `tx` from Tasks 5 and 7. Update the header table's shape. Add a test that forces the confirmation to throw after audit and asserts no audit row exists.

location: Header 'Consumes' table, `ClientOwnershipGuard` (line 55), as the authorisation for Task 4/7 routes `GET /orders/:id` and `POST /orders/:id/cancel`.
title: ClientOwnershipGuard treats `:id` as a client id, so it cannot protect order routes
failure_scenario: src/auth/guards/client-ownership.guard.ts compares `req.params.clientId ?? req.params.id` with the JWT `sub`. On `/orders/:id` that param is an ORDER id, so a client asking for their own order gets 403. The implementer's natural fix is to drop the guard from those routes. If the service then loads the order with `findUnique({ where: { id } })` without filtering by clientId, client B can read client A's order, including address and phone snapshots, and cancel it. That is an IDOR no test in the plan would notice.
fix: State in the header that ClientOwnershipGuard is only for routes whose param is a client id. Order ownership is enforced in OrdersService with `findFirst({ where: { id, ...(user.role === Role.CLIENT ? { clientId: user.sub } : {}) } })`, which returns 404 when there is no match. Add e2e tests: client B GET and cancel on client A's order → 404.

location: Task 1 schema FKs (Order→User, CartLine/OrderLine/ClientInventoryItem→Item, OrderLineAllocation/ClientBatchHolding→WarehouseBatch all default to RESTRICT). Task 1 Step 4 (lines 301-303). Task 2 new spec file. Every existing suite's cleanup chain, e.g. test/e2e/auth-login.e2e-spec.ts:30-31 and items.e2e-spec.ts:58-64.
title: New RESTRICT FKs break every existing suite's deleteMany cleanup, and the tempting fix destroys order history
failure_scenario: All 13 existing suites clean up with explicit chains (`stockMovement → warehouseBatch → item → category → … → user.deleteMany()`) that know nothing about the new tables. Step 4's 'qtyUnitsFulfilled above requested rejected' test needs a real orders row for the FK. That row persists, and the CHECK block's next beforeEach `prisma.user.deleteMany()` fails with an FK violation on orders_clientId_fkey. Every later test in the block errors. Any Phase 3 suite that leaves carts, orders, allocations or holdings behind makes items/batches/users deleteMany fail in whichever suite the sequencer runs next. The obvious 'fix' is `onDelete: Cascade` on Order→User or OrderLine→Item, which would silently delete order history and the allocation records along with it.

location: Task 1 Step 4 (lines 301-303), following the existing `.rejects.toThrow()` pattern in test/integration/search-normalisation.spec.ts.
title: The new CHECK tests pass when the CHECK is missing, and two of the six new constraints have no test
failure_scenario: The existing CHECK tests assert only `.rejects.toThrow()`. For the new ones, the insert needs a valid cart, order, batch and user. If the fixture uses gen_random_uuid() or a parent that has already been deleted, the insert fails with an FK error (23503), and the test passes even if the migration never created the CHECK. That is exactly the drift the suite exists to catch. `order_line_allocations_qty_positive` and `client_inventory_qty_non_negative` are not in the Step 4 list, so a later migrate that drops them goes unnoticed. The cart test checks only a negative quantity, so a constraint written as `>= 0` also passes. Task 3's 'PATCH to 0 removes' relies on 0 being rejected.
fix: Assert the specific constraint, e.g. `.rejects.toThrow(/cart_lines_qty_positive/)`. PostgreSQL's 23514 message names the constraint, and adapter-pg passes it through as originalMessage. Test all six (seven with the disposition CHECK) new constraints, and use boundary values: qtyBoxes 0; fulfilled = requested+1; holding −1; inventory −1; allocation 0. Add one positive control per table: a valid row is accepted.

location: Task 2 Step 1 shelf-life test (lines 355-364) and the cutoff (lines 506-507, 524). Checklist line 788 ('A batch with under 30 days' shelf life is skipped').
title: Shelf-life tests pass with a hardcoded 30, have no boundary case, and conflict with the checklist wording (adds detail to known (b))
failure_scenario: TOO_SOON=10 days and GOOD=300 days pass with the setting ignored and 30 hardcoded, or with `expiry.warnDaysAhead` (60) read by mistake. Because 10 < 30 < 60 < 300, neither mistake is caught, and an admin who later sets the minimum to 90 is silently ignored. No test pins expiry = today+N, which spec §7.3 says must be excluded because the rule is `>`. Checklist line 788 says only 'under 30 days' is skipped, which suggests exactly 30 ships. On known (b): the timezone skew window is not 'evenings'. adapter-pg sends a raw-query Date as an untyped UTC wall-clock string ('YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS'), and PostgreSQL resolves it to `date` against the DATE column. The effective rule is expiryDate > UTC-date(now+N). That trails Baghdad's date only between 00:00 and 03:00 local, and in that window a batch with exactly N days left is allowed. So a naive boundary test is flaky depending on wall-clock time.
fix:
Compute the cutoff as a business-timezone calendar date string, `today(business.timezone) + N`, and compare `"expiryDate" > ${cutoffDate}::date`. Add tests using `vi.setSystemTime`:
- set `expiry.minShelfLifeOnDeliveryDays` = 90; a 60-day batch is skipped and a 100-day batch is used;
- expiry = today+N is excluded and today+N+1 is included, with time frozen at 01:30 Asia/Baghdad.
Align the checklist wording with the spec's strict `>`.

location: Task 2 release() docstring (lines 579-581). Self-Review 'Type consistency' (line 815). Mirrors spec §7.4 line 425.
title: The 'ORDER_OUT sums to zero for a cancelled order' invariant is false for WRITTEN_OFF and is not what makes the ledger replayable
failure_scenario: WRITTEN_OFF deliberately keeps its −X ORDER_OUT, so a cancelled WRITTEN_OFF order nets −X. Replayability is per batch (Σ ADMIN movements per batch = qtyUnitsRemaining) and does not depend on per-order sums. A Phase 5 ledger-assert or a Task 7 test written from this docstring would flag every WRITTEN_OFF order as drift. The obvious 'repair' is writing +X, which fabricates exactly the stock §7.4 warns about. Release reusing ORDER_OUT with a positive delta does keep per-order sums at zero for CONFIRMED and RETURNED_TO_WAREHOUSE cancels.
fix: Reword: 'Per-batch replay stays exact. For orders cancelled with any disposition other than WRITTEN_OFF, net ORDER_OUT is zero; for WRITTEN_OFF it equals −Σ allocations, by design.' Assert that scoped form in Task 7's tests. Update the StockMovement comment ('Positive on intake and delivery') to mention release's positive ORDER_OUT.

title: Several value invariants have no CHECK
failure_scenario:
The schema accepts:
- `unitsPerBoxSnapshot = 0`: unitsToBoxes throws on every read of that order, so the order view 500s permanently.
- negative `pricePerBoxSnapshot`, `lineTotal` or `totalAmount`: a wrong cash total collected by the driver.
- `qtyBoxesRequested <= 0`.
- status/timestamp incoherence, e.g. CONFIRMED with null confirmedAt or DELIVERED with null deliveredAt. Hot deals FREQUENT and delivery windows read deliveredAt.
- Phase 4 fields: fractionalCarry outside [0,1), negative usageRateOverride, negative minQtyUnits. §7.5's carry arithmetic assumes 0 ≤ carry < 1.

location: Task 1 ClientBatchHolding (lines 219-231) and ClientInventoryItem (lines 190-212). User-side onDelete: Cascade on both, plus Cart.
title: Holdings vs. inventory invariant is undefined for Phase 4; batchId index missing; cascade deletes conflict with the ledger's SET NULL and its CHECK
failure_scenario: Nothing states whether Σ holdings(client, item) must equal ClientInventoryItem.qtyUnits, or whether holdings are a ledger-rebuildable cache. A Phase 4 stock count that finds MORE than the holdings sum, for example after auto-decrement over-drained them, has no batch to attribute the surplus to. Holdings and inventory then diverge permanently, and 'this batch expires in 20 days' (§7.5) becomes untrue. The schema claims Phase 4 needs only behaviour, not a migration. Phase 5's expiry-warnings query ('holding client' by batch) has no batchId-leading index. @@index([clientId]) duplicates the unique's leading column. The cascade is mostly dead code: stock_movements.clientId is ON DELETE SET NULL (Phase 2 migration), which violates stock_movements_owner_consistent. Any user with a CLIENT movement therefore cannot be deleted, and the cascade misstates the intended rule.
fix: Document the invariant: Σ holdings ≤ qtyUnits, with holdings as a best-effort expiry view, rebuildable from batchId-bearing CLIENT movements. Require AUTO_DECREMENT to write one movement per batch it depletes. Replace `@@index([clientId])` with `@@index([batchId])`. Use onDelete: Restrict for client-owned stock tables, or document that client users are never deleted, only suspended.

location: Task 1 HotDealEntry.kind (lines 239-240). Back-relations paragraph (line 251: `carts Cart?`). Order.placedAt (line 117) and dispatchedAt (line 119) vs spec §6 (placedAt DateTime?, no dispatchedAt).
title: Schema hygiene: free-string hot-deal kind, misnamed 1:1 back-relation, and spec drift the Self-Review claims is recorded
failure_scenario: `kind String` accepts 'Manual' or 'frequent'. Task 8's rebuild then deletes or sorts the wrong rows: a mistyped MANUAL pin is never sorted first and is never cleared by an idempotent rebuild. @@unique([itemId, kind]) also lets one item appear as both FREQUENT and NEW, so it shows twice in the carousel unless the service dedupes. `carts Cart?` is a single cart (User.carts reads as a list). The plan makes placedAt non-null @default(now()), which is better, and adds dispatchedAt, which the proposed disposition CHECK needs. Neither change is in spec §6, despite Self-Review line 811 saying spec corrections are recorded.
fix: Use `enum HotDealKind { FREQUENT NEW MANUAL }` (or a CHECK kind IN (...)) and dedupe by item in GET /hot-deals. Rename the back-relation to `cart Cart?`. Update spec §6 for placedAt, dispatchedAt, the relations and the new CHECKs.

location: Task 1 Step 3 (lines 263-269): 'Then a hand-written migration' with no command.
title: No command is given for creating the hand-written CHECK migration
failure_scenario: The most direct reading is to paste the SQL into the `ordering` migration that `migrate dev` just applied. Prisma then sees a checksum mismatch on an applied migration and demands a reset: an interactive prompt that hangs, as RESUME.md records for the Phase 2 drift prompt. Alternatively, the dev and test databases end up with different constraint sets, because the test DB replays the edited file via global-setup's `migrate deploy`.
fix: Specify: `npx prisma migrate dev --create-only --name ordering_checks`, paste the SQL into the new file, `npx prisma migrate dev`, then confirm `npx prisma migrate diff --from-config-datasource --to-schema prisma/schema.prisma --script` prints an empty migration.

location: Task 2 concurrency test (lines 405-434) and Step 5 (lines 627-633). This adds a fix to known issue (a).
title: Detail on known (a): a deterministic interleaving and a stronger assertion make Step 5 demonstrable with the CHECK still in place
failure_scenario: Besides the CHECK masking the bug, the two transactions are not forced to overlap. Each first awaits settings.get on another connection, so tx1 can commit before tx2's SELECT and the run is effectively serial. The assertions (sum ≤ 300, remaining ≥ 0) also hold when tx2 is rejected, so they cannot tell 'locked and serialised' from 'raced and rolled back'.
fix: Force the overlap: start tx1 with `prisma.$transaction(async tx => { await svc.allocate(tx, …); signal(); await tx.$executeRaw`SELECT pg_sleep(0.3)`; })`, await `signal`, then start tx2. Assert `results.every(r => r.status === 'fulfilled')` and that the allocated amounts, sorted, equal [100, 200]. With FOR UPDATE, tx2 blocks, then re-reads 100 and takes it. Without the lock, tx2 reads 300, tries −200 and is rejected by the CHECK, so the assertion fails even though the CHECK is present.
